name: Chromosome 9 Study Desk
subtitle: Understand the evidence. Explain the study.
studyTitle: Chromosome 9 Variant Annotation Profiles Across Public Acute Leukemia Sequencing Datasets

topics.title: Why chromosome 9?
topics.summary: This study describes chromosome 9 annotation patterns across public acute leukemia sequencing runs.
topics.why: The chromosome contains leukemia-associated loci, but a gene label alone does not establish a pathogenic alteration.
topics.detail: The introduction connects chromosome 9 to leukemia research through PAX5 and neighbouring loci. The study asks how recovered gene assignments and coding summaries compare across heterogeneous public runs. It describes annotations rather than establishing a clinical test or a causal disease mechanism. Literature findings reported in the manuscript provide context, not validation of these particular records.
topics.evidence: The manuscript discusses PAX5-related literature and reports PAX5-associated records in both AML and ALL summaries.
topics.misconception: A known leukemia-associated gene makes every record assigned to it pathogenic. Gene relevance and the effect of a particular allele are different questions.
topics.example: PAX5 in both groups means both recovered annotation sets contain PAX5 assignments. It does not establish that the same allele occurs in both.
topics.poster: Introduction and Objective; Results and Discussion
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: What kind of study is this?
topics.summary: A secondary descriptive analysis of six sequencing runs, not a review article or a recruited patient cohort.
topics.why: The analytical unit determines which conclusions are defensible. Six runs are not six independent patients.
topics.detail: The authors retrieved public DNA sequencing inputs and compared annotation profiles. The sequencing run was the analytical unit. The study did not estimate patient mutation prevalence, clinical performance or between-group statistical significance. The manuscript contains a literature review section, but that section does not make the whole study a systematic or narrative review.
topics.evidence: Six runs represented four BioSample identifiers. The three ALL runs shared one REH source.
topics.misconception: Three ALL runs and three AML runs mean two independent clinical cohorts of three patients each.
topics.example: Treating different platforms measuring REH as independent patients would exaggerate biological replication.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Six runs, four biological sources
topics.summary: The ALL group repeats one REH BioSample. AML inputs differ in biological material and assay purpose.
topics.why: A profile can differ because of the source or assay, even when the disease label is unchanged.
topics.detail: ALL-1, ALL-2 and ALL-3 share SAMN13831871 and use PromethION, PacBio Sequel II and Illumina HiSeq X. AML-1 is ML-2 from a control/decitabine study. AML-2 is an HL-60 apoptotic DNA-fragment library after 24 hours at room temperature. AML-3 is bone-marrow DNA studied by sparse sequencing for copy-number quantification. These inputs are not biologically or technically equivalent.
topics.evidence: Table 1 identifies the run accessions and four BioSamples. The three AML BioSamples are SAMN02709918, SAMN34434777 and SAMN17383328.
topics.misconception: The label AML makes all three AML assays interchangeable.
topics.example: The HL-60 fragment library captures apoptosis-related DNA fragments rather than the same measurement design as dense genomic small-variant profiling.
steps: Identify the library purpose and sequencing platform.
Check whether runs share a BioSample.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: From public reads to an alignment
topics.summary: Quality assessment, trimming, assembly checks and chromosome-focused alignment precede annotation.
topics.why: Downstream annotation depends on which sequences survive processing and how well they represent the reference.
topics.detail: The reported workflow uses FastQC in Galaxy, Trimmomatic, SPAdes and QUAST. The manuscript states Q30 filtering, a 50 bp minimum read length and retained contigs of at least 500 bp. Reads and assembly-derived sequences were imported into Geneious and aligned to chromosome 9 at medium sensitivity. Platform-specific command settings and complete intermediate files are not supplied, so the paper is not a fully executable pipeline specification.
topics.misconception: Naming several tools proves every platform received an optimal or identical valid workflow.
topics.example: The presence of long-read and short-read platforms is a reason to ask how processing was adapted to each input.
steps: Align reads and assembly-derived sequences to chromosome 9.
Transfer reference annotations and examine coverage.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Identity is not coverage
topics.summary: ALL-1 had 91.4% pairwise identity but only 0.8% chromosome 9 reference coverage.
topics.why: Good agreement in a small observed region does not tell us what lies in the unobserved remainder.
topics.detail: Pairwise identity concerns sequence agreement within an alignment. Reference coverage concerns how much of the chromosome reference is represented. ALL-1 had a reported maximum coverage of 3. Sparse representation restricts claims about absence of annotations elsewhere. The manuscript also reports 328,321 reads entering the analysis, with 326 assigned to the assembled component and 327,995 unassembled. Do not interpret reference feature counts as detected mutations.
topics.evidence: ALL-1: identity 91.4%; reference coverage 0.8%; maximum coverage 3.
topics.misconception: High pairwise identity means the whole chromosome has been adequately sampled.
topics.example: Think of checking a small paragraph against a book: a good match in that paragraph is not evidence that every page was checked. This is an analogy, not a study measurement.
steps: Ask how well aligned sequences agree.
Separately ask how much reference was observed.
Restrict absence claims to adequately observed regions.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Calling thresholds versus group tests
topics.summary: Geneious filter settings are not tests of AML–ALL differences.
topics.why: A small calling P-value cannot establish disease-group enrichment.
topics.detail: The manuscript reports an approximate minimum variant frequency of 0.6, a maximum variant P-value below 0.001 and a strand-bias P-value threshold of 10⁻⁶. Strand bias above 65% was flagged. These settings were used for detection and filtering. Their precise software implementation must be checked in the analysis records before reproducing the workflow. All between-group comparisons were descriptive.
topics.evidence: No between-group significance test, confidence interval or clinical performance estimate is reported.
topics.misconception: P < 0.001 in the calling method means AML has significantly more mutations than ALL.
topics.example: A setting governing whether an individual candidate is retained answers a different question from a test comparing two groups.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Annotation records versus validated variants
topics.summary: An annotation record is an annotated entry used in the summaries, not automatically an independent somatic mutation.
topics.why: Counting records, assigning genes and proving pathogenicity are different analytical tasks.
topics.detail: Reference annotations assign context such as genes and coding sequences to aligned differences. Multiple records can relate to the same locus or allele. Gene assignment does not establish a fusion, functional disruption or clinical classification. The reference layer contained 2,487 gene features, 5,514 coding-sequence features, 5,505 messenger RNA features, 1,636 noncoding RNA features and 6,270 regulatory features. Those are reference features, not counts of altered genes or expressed transcripts.
topics.evidence: PAX5 entries were present in both groups; NUP214 in ALL and NOTCH1 in AML summaries. The study does not establish specific pathogenic lesions or fusions.
topics.misconception: A reference gene feature count equals the number of variant-bearing genes.
topics.example: A file label pointing to NUP214 is not proof of a NUP214 fusion.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: What do the annotation counts show?
topics.summary: AML-associated counts had a higher median and wider range, with overlap between groups.
topics.why: Describe the observed pattern without converting it into a prevalence estimate or significance claim.
topics.detail: The ALL run-level range was 4–4,943 and its median 92. The AML range was 25–8,117 and its median 1,822. Each group has three sequencing runs, but the ALL runs share one source. These are annotation-record counts. With heterogeneous assays and sparse coverage, a larger record count cannot be read directly as greater biological disease burden.
topics.evidence: ALL median 92, AML median 1,822; ranges overlap. Figure 1 displays the distributions.
topics.misconception: The bigger AML median proves a significant difference or greater clinical mutation burden.
topics.example: A defensible oral sentence is: “AML-associated record counts were higher and more dispersed in this collection, with overlapping ranges.”
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Protein effects and amino-acid summaries
topics.summary: Substitutions predominated in both groups. Truncation labels were more prominent in ALL.
topics.why: Predicted consequence labels suggest follow-up questions but do not prove a protein-level mechanism.
topics.detail: Proline-to-leucine led the ALL-associated top-ten amino-acid-change summary, while glycine-to-arginine led AML. Proline-to-leucine, glutamate-to-lysine, alanine-to-valine and alanine-to-threonine appeared in both top-ten lists. These categories are pooled across coding sequences and do not identify a specific protein domain or recurrent allele. Sequence-change classes are a separate annotation layer and should not be conflated with protein-effect categories.
topics.evidence: Figures 3 and 4 show protein-effect and amino-acid categories. Exact numerical chart data are not supplied in a machine-readable table.
topics.misconception: A frequent pooled amino-acid change identifies a common functional driver in one gene.
topics.example: Proline-to-leucine can occur in unrelated proteins. A shared category is not necessarily a shared genomic alteration.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Why pooled positions are not hotspots
topics.summary: Codon and coding-position labels are pooled across coding sequences, not chromosome coordinates.
topics.why: The same number can refer to positions in many different proteins or transcripts.
topics.detail: The leading codon-number labels were 151 in ALL and 539 in AML. The leading coding-sequence-position labels were 1074 and 1327, respectively. To establish recurrence, one would need a normalized alteration in a specified gene and transcript across independent samples. Table 2 lists selected position categories in ascending numerical order rather than frequency order.
topics.evidence: ALL: leading codon 151 and coding-position 1074. AML: 539 and 1327.
topics.misconception: The most prominent pooled codon label is a chromosome 9 mutation hotspot.
topics.example: Codon 151 in one gene and codon 151 in another are different molecular positions.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Shared and group-restricted sets
topics.summary: Few recovered labels or annotation records were shared between the two pooled groups.
topics.why: A recovered-set difference describes these data; it does not establish biological exclusivity.
topics.detail: Gene-label overlap comprised 196 AML-only, 15 shared and 41 ALL-only labels. Variant annotation-record overlap comprised 742 AML-only, 4 shared and 551 ALL-only entries. These are separate set comparisons with different units. Sparse coverage, different assay purposes and annotation handling may contribute to low overlap. Do not derive a proportion without specifying which set and denominator it refers to.
topics.evidence: Figure 5: gene labels 196 / 15 / 41; annotation records 742 / 4 / 551 (AML-only / shared / ALL-only).
topics.misconception: AML-only entries are validated leukemia-specific biomarkers or proven absent from ALL.
topics.example: “Group-restricted in the recovered profiles” is more accurate than “unique to all AML genomes.”
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Why clustering does not separate the groups
topics.summary: AML and ALL labels intermix. ALL-3 and AML-2 form the closest pair.
topics.why: A dendrogram summarizes similarity in a chosen feature representation, not diagnostic accuracy.
topics.detail: ALL-1, ALL-2 and AML-3 joined the ALL-3/AML-2 pair successively, while AML-1 joined last. Correlation distance and average linkage were used. Branch height represents clustering distance, not statistical support. Mixed labels do not imply that AML and ALL are genomically indistinguishable. Biological source, assay design, coverage and feature processing all limit interpretation.
topics.evidence: Figures 6 and 7 both pair ALL-3 with AML-2.
topics.misconception: The closest pair has the same biology, or the dendrogram proves that leukemia types are indistinguishable.
topics.example: One ALL run can resemble an AML run in the recovered annotation matrix without erasing biological distinctions between leukemia types.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: Reading the clustered heat map
topics.summary: Rows are six runs, columns are genes, and values show the plotted annotation representation.
topics.why: Colour is meaningful only with its scale and preprocessing, not as a direct clinical measure.
topics.detail: The manuscript reports row-wise unit-variance scaling, missing-value imputation, correlation distance and average linkage. The figure caption describes a displayed 0–1 colour scale. Those statements do not fully document how standardized values became the plotted range. The exact transformation and imputation details need the analysis code or original matrix. Do not infer raw counts, expression or disease severity from colour alone.
topics.evidence: Figure 7 intersperses AML and ALL labels and pairs ALL-3 with AML-2.
topics.misconception: A green cell means increased gene expression, or a displayed 0–1 value is necessarily a raw mutation frequency.
topics.example: A colour scale is a visual encoding of processed matrix values. Ask what operation produced those values before assigning a biological interpretation.
topics.poster: Clustering summarized; heat map not displayed
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: What the evidence cannot establish
topics.summary: The study supports descriptive annotation comparisons, with substantial design and coverage limitations.
topics.why: Good discussion depends as much on the boundary of a claim as on the observed numbers.
topics.detail: The collection is small, its three ALL runs share a source, and the AML assays differ. ALL-1 reference representation is sparse. Records may not be independent alleles. There is no matched normal comparison, functional validation or clinical outcome analysis. These issues restrict leukemia-specific, mechanistic and biomarker conclusions. Source accession transparency and a defined reference are strengths, but do not remove those limits.
topics.evidence: The discussion explicitly calls for independent samples, suitable platform-specific processing, justified callable regions and allele-level normalization.
topics.misconception: Listing limitations means the descriptive findings have no value. Their value is bounded, not erased.
topics.example: A useful contribution is a traceable chromosome-focused description that motivates more controlled comparisons.
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

topics.title: A defensible oral synthesis
topics.summary: Different recovered profiles, limited overlap and mixed clustering support further controlled study.
topics.why: A concise synthesis should connect the observations to their limits and a realistic next step.
topics.detail: Explain the purpose, identify the six-run/four-BioSample design, describe the count and overlap patterns, then state why the findings remain descriptive. Do not describe a validated leukemia-specific signature, a causal mechanism or a clinical biomarker. Recommend independent biological sources, adequate callable coverage and normalized gene/transcript-level alleles before functional or clinical validation.
topics.evidence: The conclusion reports variable chromosome 9 profiles, predominant substitutions, limited set overlap, mixed run-level clustering and PAX5 records in both groups.
topics.misconception: The title must be defended as a discovery of disease-specific pathogenic variants.
topics.example: “We describe heterogeneous chromosome 9 annotation profiles in public leukemia-associated runs. Provenance and coverage limit disease-level interpretation.”
topics.support: Faithful paraphrase; plain-language explanations are educational interpretations.

flashcards.front: Why chromosome 9?
flashcards.back: This study describes chromosome 9 annotation patterns across public acute leukemia sequencing runs. The chromosome contains leukemia-associated loci, but a gene label alone does not establish a pathogenic alteration.

flashcards.front: What kind of study is this?
flashcards.back: A secondary descriptive analysis of six sequencing runs, not a review article or a recruited patient cohort. The analytical unit determines which conclusions are defensible. Six runs are not six independent patients.

flashcards.front: Six runs, four biological sources
flashcards.back: The ALL group repeats one REH BioSample. AML inputs differ in biological material and assay purpose. A profile can differ because of the source or assay, even when the disease label is unchanged.

flashcards.front: From public reads to an alignment
flashcards.back: Quality assessment, trimming, assembly checks and chromosome-focused alignment precede annotation. Downstream annotation depends on which sequences survive processing and how well they represent the reference.

flashcards.front: Identity is not coverage
flashcards.back: ALL-1 had 91.4% pairwise identity but only 0.8% chromosome 9 reference coverage. Good agreement in a small observed region does not tell us what lies in the unobserved remainder.

flashcards.front: Calling thresholds versus group tests
flashcards.back: Geneious filter settings are not tests of AML–ALL differences. A small calling P-value cannot establish disease-group enrichment.

flashcards.front: Annotation records versus validated variants
flashcards.back: An annotation record is an annotated entry used in the summaries, not automatically an independent somatic mutation. Counting records, assigning genes and proving pathogenicity are different analytical tasks.

flashcards.front: What do the annotation counts show?
flashcards.back: AML-associated counts had a higher median and wider range, with overlap between groups. Describe the observed pattern without converting it into a prevalence estimate or significance claim.

flashcards.front: Protein effects and amino-acid summaries
flashcards.back: Substitutions predominated in both groups. Truncation labels were more prominent in ALL. Predicted consequence labels suggest follow-up questions but do not prove a protein-level mechanism.

flashcards.front: Why pooled positions are not hotspots
flashcards.back: Codon and coding-position labels are pooled across coding sequences, not chromosome coordinates. The same number can refer to positions in many different proteins or transcripts.

flashcards.front: Shared and group-restricted sets
flashcards.back: Few recovered labels or annotation records were shared between the two pooled groups. A recovered-set difference describes these data; it does not establish biological exclusivity.

flashcards.front: Why clustering does not separate the groups
flashcards.back: AML and ALL labels intermix. ALL-3 and AML-2 form the closest pair. A dendrogram summarizes similarity in a chosen feature representation, not diagnostic accuracy.

flashcards.front: Reading the clustered heat map
flashcards.back: Rows are six runs, columns are genes, and values show the plotted annotation representation. Colour is meaningful only with its scale and preprocessing, not as a direct clinical measure.

flashcards.front: What the evidence cannot establish
flashcards.back: The study supports descriptive annotation comparisons, with substantial design and coverage limitations. Good discussion depends as much on the boundary of a claim as on the observed numbers.

flashcards.front: A defensible oral synthesis
flashcards.back: Different recovered profiles, limited overlap and mixed clustering support further controlled study. A concise synthesis should connect the observations to their limits and a realistic next step.

flashcards.front: Explain Chromosome 9 in this study.
flashcards.back: The chromosome reference selected for this comparison. Same reference, different recovered profiles.

flashcards.front: Explain PAX5 in this study.
flashcards.back: A gene label discussed in the leukemia literature and found in both study groups. Gene name is context, not a verdict.

flashcards.front: Explain Annotation record in this study.
flashcards.back: An annotated entry included in the descriptive summaries. Record count is not automatically mutation count.

flashcards.front: Explain Allele in this study.
flashcards.back: A particular version of sequence at a specified locus. Which change, at which site?

flashcards.front: Explain Sequencing run in this study.
flashcards.back: One sequencing data acquisition identified by a run accession. A run is a measurement, not necessarily a new sample.

flashcards.front: Explain BioSample in this study.
flashcards.back: An identifier describing the biological source of archived sequence data. Count sources separately from runs.

flashcards.front: Explain REH in this study.
flashcards.back: The leukemia cell-line source represented by all three ALL runs. Three platforms, one REH source.

flashcards.front: Explain Biological replication in this study.
flashcards.back: Independent biological sources, as distinct from repeated measurement of one source. More runs need not mean more biology.

flashcards.front: Explain Sequencing library in this study.
flashcards.back: The prepared sequence material measured by a sequencing experiment. Preparation shapes what you can observe.

flashcards.front: Explain Read in this study.
flashcards.back: A sequence observation obtained by sequencing. Observed sequence first, interpretation later.

flashcards.front: Explain Q30 in this study.
flashcards.back: The quality-filtering threshold described in the methods. Quality does not replace coverage.

flashcards.front: Explain Contig in this study.
flashcards.back: An assembled contiguous sequence used in the reported processing workflow. Assembled stretch of sequence.

flashcards.front: Explain Reference sequence in this study.
flashcards.back: The sequence used as the alignment and annotation coordinate context. A coordinate framework, not a patient measurement.

flashcards.front: Explain Pairwise identity in this study.
flashcards.back: Agreement between the sequences being aligned. Match quality and observed extent are different.

flashcards.front: Explain Reference coverage in this study.
flashcards.back: How much of the chromosome reference is represented by the aligned sequences. How much did we actually observe?

flashcards.front: Explain Callable region in this study.
flashcards.back: A region sufficiently observed for a justified variant comparison. No observation is not proof of no variant.

flashcards.front: Explain Variant-frequency setting in this study.
flashcards.back: A calling setting used to retain candidate differences in Geneious. Caller rule, not cohort result.

flashcards.front: Explain Strand bias in this study.
flashcards.back: Uneven representation of a candidate difference across sequence strands, considered during filtering. Check evidence symmetry before interpretation.

flashcards.front: Explain Calling P-value in this study.
flashcards.back: A statistical quantity used within the variant-calling/filtering procedure. Ask which question the P-value belongs to.

flashcards.front: Explain Descriptive analysis in this study.
flashcards.back: A summary of observed patterns without the reported between-group significance testing or clinical-performance estimation. Describe the collection before generalizing.

flashcards.front: Explain Somatic variant in this study.
flashcards.back: A sequence alteration arising in somatic cells, distinct from inherited variation. Annotation alone does not prove somatic origin.

flashcards.front: Explain Transcript context in this study.
flashcards.back: The RNA/coding-sequence reference context used to describe a predicted effect. Name the transcript before naming the consequence.

flashcards.front: Explain Median in this study.
flashcards.back: The middle value after ordering the observations. Middle, not average.

flashcards.front: Explain Predicted substitution in this study.
flashcards.back: A predicted protein-effect category predominant in both groups. Predicted label first, validation later.

flashcards.front: Explain Predicted truncation in this study.
flashcards.back: An annotation predicting a shortened protein product. A predicted shorter product, not a proven phenotype.

flashcards.front: Explain Frameshift in this study.
flashcards.back: A coding consequence that changes how downstream codons are read. Shift the reading frame, then inspect the context.

flashcards.front: Explain Codon label in this study.
flashcards.back: A position label within a coding sequence, pooled here across coding sequences. A number needs a gene and transcript.

flashcards.front: Explain Mutational hotspot in this study.
flashcards.back: A recurrent alteration region requiring defined molecular context and suitable independent evidence. Recurrence needs a precise address.

flashcards.front: Explain Annotation set in this study.
flashcards.back: A collection of recovered labels or records used for overlap comparison. Specify what a set contains.

flashcards.front: Explain Dendrogram in this study.
flashcards.back: A tree showing the order and distances of clustering merges. A similarity tree, not a diagnosis.

flashcards.front: Explain Correlation distance in this study.
flashcards.back: The similarity-related distance used for the reported clustering. Close in this matrix, under this rule.

flashcards.front: Explain Average linkage in this study.
flashcards.back: The merge rule used to build the reported hierarchical clustering. Distance plus merge rule makes a tree.

flashcards.front: Explain Heat map in this study.
flashcards.back: A coloured display of the processed run-by-gene annotation matrix. Read the legend and transformation first.

flashcards.front: Explain Row-wise scaling in this study.
flashcards.back: The reported transformation of run-level profiles before heat-map analysis. Transformed values are not automatically raw frequencies.

flashcards.front: Explain Missing-value imputation in this study.
flashcards.back: Filling missing entries as part of matrix processing. A filled value needs a stated rule.

flashcards.front: Explain Clinical biomarker in this study.
flashcards.back: A measurable feature with evidence supporting a defined clinical use. A candidate pattern is a starting point.

flashcards.front: Explain AML in this study.
flashcards.back: The disease-associated label used for three included sequencing runs. Disease label plus provenance.

flashcards.front: Explain ALL in this study.
flashcards.back: The disease-associated label used for the three REH runs. Three ALL runs, one source.

flashcards.front: Explain SRA in this study.
flashcards.back: A public archive used to obtain the sequencing inputs. Archive accessions support traceability.

flashcards.front: Explain ENA in this study.
flashcards.back: Another archive used for the public sequence data. Locate the archived source before interpreting it.

flashcards.front: Explain Geneious in this study.
flashcards.back: The software used for chromosome 9 alignment, calling and annotation in the reported workflow. Tool name is not a full reproducible protocol.

slides.title: Background and objective
slides.message: This study describes chromosome 9 annotation patterns across public acute leukemia sequencing runs.
slides.guide: The introduction connects chromosome 9 to leukemia research through PAX5 and neighbouring loci. The study asks how recovered gene assignments and coding summaries compare across heterogeneous public runs. It describes annotations rather than establishing a clinical test or a causal disease mechanism. Literature findings reported in the manuscript provide context, not validation of these particular records.

slides.title: Sequencing datasets
slides.message: A secondary descriptive analysis of six sequencing runs, not a review article or a recruited patient cohort.
slides.guide: The authors retrieved public DNA sequencing inputs and compared annotation profiles. The sequencing run was the analytical unit. The study did not estimate patient mutation prevalence, clinical performance or between-group statistical significance. The manuscript contains a literature review section, but that section does not make the whole study a systematic or narrative review.

slides.title: Methods and coverage
slides.message: Quality assessment, trimming, assembly checks and chromosome-focused alignment precede annotation.
slides.guide: The reported workflow uses FastQC in Galaxy, Trimmomatic, SPAdes and QUAST. The manuscript states Q30 filtering, a 50 bp minimum read length and retained contigs of at least 500 bp. Reads and assembly-derived sequences were imported into Geneious and aligned to chromosome 9 at medium sensitivity. Platform-specific command settings and complete intermediate files are not supplied, so the paper is not a fully executable pipeline specification.

slides.title: Coding-annotation patterns
slides.message: Substitutions predominated in both groups. Truncation labels were more prominent in ALL.
slides.guide: Proline-to-leucine led the ALL-associated top-ten amino-acid-change summary, while glycine-to-arginine led AML. Proline-to-leucine, glutamate-to-lysine, alanine-to-valine and alanine-to-threonine appeared in both top-ten lists. These categories are pooled across coding sequences and do not identify a specific protein domain or recurrent allele. Sequence-change classes are a separate annotation layer and should not be conflated with protein-effect categories.

slides.title: Annotation-set overlap
slides.message: Few recovered labels or annotation records were shared between the two pooled groups.
slides.guide: Gene-label overlap comprised 196 AML-only, 15 shared and 41 ALL-only labels. Variant annotation-record overlap comprised 742 AML-only, 4 shared and 551 ALL-only entries. These are separate set comparisons with different units. Sparse coverage, different assay purposes and annotation handling may contribute to low overlap. Do not derive a proportion without specifying which set and denominator it refers to.

slides.message: AML and ALL labels intermix. ALL-3 and AML-2 form the closest pair.
slides.guide: ALL-1, ALL-2 and AML-3 joined the ALL-3/AML-2 pair successively, while AML-1 joined last. Correlation distance and average linkage were used. Branch height represents clustering distance, not statistical support. Mixed labels do not imply that AML and ALL are genomically indistinguishable. Biological source, assay design, coverage and feature processing all limit interpretation.

slides.title: Conclusion and limits
slides.message: The study supports descriptive annotation comparisons, with substantial design and coverage limitations.
slides.guide: The collection is small, its three ALL runs share a source, and the AML assays differ. ALL-1 reference representation is sparse. Records may not be independent alleles. There is no matched normal comparison, functional validation or clinical outcome analysis. These issues restrict leukemia-specific, mechanistic and biomarker conclusions. Source accession transparency and a defined reference are strengths, but do not remove those limits.

slides.answer: Listing limitations means the descriptive findings have no value. Their value is bounded, not erased.

slides.message: Identify selected literature and distinguish contextual evidence from this study’s records.

slides.question: What would be an overinterpretation of this slide?
slides.answer: A known leukemia-associated gene makes every record assigned to it pathogenic. Gene relevance and the effect of a particular allele are different questions.

discrepancies.title: Study type
discrepancies.detail: The build prompt calls this a review. The supplied manuscript is a secondary descriptive data analysis; a literature-review section is background.

discrepancies.title: Legacy figure terminology
discrepancies.detail: Several embedded figure titles use mutation, mutation burden or mutation profiles. The manuscript defines the summaries as annotation records rather than validated distinct somatic mutations.

discrepancies.title: Heat-map transformation
discrepancies.detail: Row-wise unit-variance scaling is reported, while the caption describes a 0–1 display. The exact transformation and imputation details require the original matrix/code.

discrepancies.title: Presentation compression
discrepancies.detail: The oral and poster summaries omit many tool settings, coding-position lists and references. The manuscript remains the authority; omissions are not contradictory results.

discrepancies.title: Missing contact/slot
discrepancies.detail: No corresponding-author email or assigned slot was supplied. Neither was invented.
